context: Current closing price of Verizon (VZ): $42.88 USD as of 2026-07-15.
justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across time horizons, starting near current market levels and gradually trending higher. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of roughly 42.95 is anchored closely to the prevailing price, assuming mean-reverting intraday dynamics with little new fundamental information likely to arrive overnight. At the one-week horizon, the slight uptick to 43.10 reflects a mild positive drift assumption, consistent with modest bullish momentum or carry effects that tend to persist over short windows. At the one-month horizon, the estimate of 43.50 incorporates a somewhat larger expected drift, acknowledging that over longer periods, assets with positive expected returns tend to trend upward in the absence of major adverse shocks. All three estimates essentially assume a relatively calm environment with no major regime change.

The confidence interval widths grow substantially as the horizon extends, which reflects the standard square-root-of-time scaling of uncertainty in financial markets. At one day, the 90% interval of roughly 41.80 to 44.10 is tight because very little time passes for new information to accumulate and prices to deviate far from their starting point. At one week, the interval widens to 41.00–45.20, capturing the greater variety of macro data releases, central bank communications, and sentiment shifts that could occur. By one month, the interval of 39.50–47.50 is considerably wider, reflecting the compounding of daily uncertainties and the higher probability of encountering a meaningful trend shift or volatility event within that window.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals entirely. On the downside, a surprise deterioration in macroeconomic data, an unexpected central bank policy tightening, or a geopolitical shock could generate sharp selling pressure that breaks below the lower bound of even the one-month interval. Liquidity crises or correlated risk-off moves across asset classes can produce tail moves far larger than historical volatility would imply. On the upside, a strong earnings beat, a dovish policy pivot, or a short-squeeze dynamic could drive prices well above the upper bounds. The stated intervals assume roughly log-normal return distributions, which historically underestimate the frequency and magnitude of true fat-tail events, so real-world outcomes in the tails may be more common than the 10% combined probability implies.
